newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian protesters again occupy port city centre.
newsitem.headline: Albanian protesters again occupy port city centre.

text.p: Tens of thousands of Albanians, blaming the government for collapsed investment schemes, swept aside lines of riot police on Thursday to occupy the centre of this port city for the second consecutive day.
Up to 30,000 protesters, their numbers swelled throughout the morning by villagers impoverished by the collapsed schemes, poured jubilantly through city streets to Independence Square.

"Vlore is ours, down with the government," the crowd chanted, punching the air and demanding the resignation of President Sali Berisha's right-wing government. "Sali, you thief, where have you put our money?" others shouted.

The protests, sparked by the collapse of one scheme based in the area, engulfed the centre of the city throughout Wednesday. Police fought pitched battles with demonstrators down palm-lined boulevards, but twice failed to disperse them.
The interior ministry said three demonstrators and three policemen were injured in Wednesday's clashes. The country's most popular newspaper, Koha Jone, said 20 people were hurt.
Riot policemen told Reuter correspondents at least 25 officers had suffered facial injuries from flying stones. Several said they were tired of confronting the demonstrators.

Berisha has offered limited help to ruined despositors, particularly those who sold homes to increase their stake. In an interview published on Thursday he said his opponents had failed in their aim of turning discontent into a bloodbath.
"The opposition made a big mistake. It wanted a bloodbath and it did not happen," Berisha told the Paris daily Le Monde. "Albania is calm."

Women and children led Thursday's ragged procession down streets of the Adriatic port as police moved out of their way. Some protesters went to a high school and persuaded pupils to leave classrooms and join the rally.
About 10,000 protesters surged to the main police station early in the afternoon and demanded the release of comrades they said had been detained during Wednesday's skirmishes.

"Free our friends," shouted the protesters, massed in the street and on nearby balconies and rooftops. Riot police guarding the building crouched or raised their shields to protect themselves against a hail of stones.
Two attempts by several hundred protesters to push past the guards were repulsed. Police initially denied holding anyone but later released about 20 people.
The crowds had dispersed in the early afternoon but vowed to regroup after nightfall.

The protests were the first since angry depositors set fire to public buildings in several cities last month. More than 150 people were arrested after those disturbances and prosecutors pledged to seek minimum 15-year jail terms.
Virtually every family has invested money in the schemes in the six years since Albania emerged from eastern Europe's most repressive communist regime.
Partial refunds are being dispensed for two failed pyramid schemes but many depositors are angry that they are not getting their entire stake back.
Some accuse the ruling Democratic Party, founded by Berisha, of using the proceeds to finance its re-election in polls last year, denounced as rigged by Western observers.

Gjallica, based in Vlore, owed depositors an estimated $500 million and was the fifth major pyramid scheme to go bankrupt since November. A small number of other investment schemes are clinging to life, although they have cut interest payments.
Economists believe as much as $2 billion was tied up altogether and say the inevitable collapse of other companies could pitch Albania into uncontrollable violence.
